n18: Biblical meditation means softly muttering a verse again and again, letting it sink in.

n20: Read it aloud slowly, three times
n21: Mutter it softly, stressing a different word each time ("The LORD is my shepherd…")
n22: Ask: "What is God saying to me through this?"

n30: The Hebrew word hagah (Ps 1:2; Josh 1:8) means to murmur or mutter. Slow, rhythmic speech slows breathing and replaces worried rumination with truth.
n31: In the Bible, to meditate means to say a verse softly again and again, like chewing your food slowly. It helps God's words go deep into your heart.
n34: Pray a short phrase in rhythm with your breathing.

n36: Breathe in slowly through your nose with the first half
n37: Breathe out longer than you breathe in with the second half
n38: Repeat for two to five minutes

n45: Simple is the point: prayer your body can do
n46: Pairing a long exhale with a short repeated phrase slows breathing to about six breaths a minute, which strengthens the heart's calming reflex (Bernardi 2001).
n47: Breathe in and say a few words to God, breathe out and say a few more. Slow breaths and short prayers calm your body and bring you close to God.

n61: Focus on God, not on the experience
n62: In a small 2006 brain-scan study (Newberg), activity in the frontal lobes, which control deliberate speech and self-monitoring, dropped during tongues while people stayed aware. Another small study found lower stress markers after group worship that included tongues.
n63: Some Christians pray in a special prayer language from the Holy Spirit. It helps them pour out their heart to God without worrying about the right words.
n66: Sing or hum songs of worship, alone or with others.

n77: Sing a psalm or a song you remember
n78: Singing lengthens the out-breath and vibrates the throat, which engages the vagus nerve. When people sing together, their heart rates can synchronise (Vickhoff 2013).
n79: Singing to God fills your heart with joy and makes your body calm, especially when you sing with other people.

n114: Set aside food or something else for a set time to seek God.

n116: Choose what and how long (one meal, a day, or a non-food fast such as social media)

n119: Break the fast gently and give thanks
n121: Stop and eat; health matters more
n123: Turn each hunger pang into a short prayer
n126: Short fasts trigger hunger signals that can sharpen attention for prayer. Fasting from screens frees attention and lowers the constant reward-seeking of the dopamine system.
n127: Do not fast from food if you have diabetes, an eating disorder history, are pregnant or breastfeeding, are a child, or are unwell. Choose a non-food fast instead.
n128: Fasting means going without something, like a meal or your phone, for a short time, to spend that time with God. Always be safe and ask a grown-up or doctor first.

n145: Detachment or a state of emptiness

n153: Scripture fills the heart rather than emptying it
n154: Christian meditation fills your mind with God and His words. Mindfulness helps you notice the present. Emptying the mind tries to think of nothing. The Bible invites us to be filled, not empty.
n155: Silence switches off a lot of the input that keeps the alarm system busy. Breathing and heart rate slow, and the mind has space to settle.
n156: God speaks in the still, small voice. Stillness is not emptiness; it is attention to a Person who is already present.
